sec.title: Question
sec.p: Does first-line tislelizumab plus chemotherapy improve long-term outcomes compared with placebo plus chemotherapy in participants with recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal cancer?

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: In this randomized clinical trial including 263 participants, tislelizumab plus chemotherapy demonstrated sustained progression-free survival benefit (median, 9.6 months vs 7.4 months) and clinically meaningful overall survival improvement (median, 45.3 months vs 31.8 months) compared with placebo plus chemotherapy after 3 years of follow-up, which is consistent with the interim analysis.

sec.title: Meaning
sec.p: These findings support tislelizumab plus chemotherapy as a first-line treatment for recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal cancer, with the potential to provide sustained, long-term survival benefit.

abstract.p: This secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial evaluates the 3-year efficacy and safety of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy vs placebo plus chemotherapy in participants with recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma and explores potential biomarkers of treatment response.

sec.title: Importance
sec.p: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a major health concern in Asia, and treatment options for recurrent or metastatic disease are limited. Immunotherapy plus chemotherapy has shown promise, but long-term data are needed to guide first-line treatment.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To evaluate the 3-year efficacy and safety of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy vs placebo plus chemotherapy in participants with recurrent or metastatic NPC and explore potential biomarkers of treatment response.

sec.title: Design, Setting, and Participants
sec.p: The RATIONALE-309 trial was a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 randomized clinical trial conducted in Asia from April 2019 to December 2023. Treatment-naive adults with histologically or cytologically confirmed recurrent or metastatic NPC were included. Data were analyzed from December 2023 to January 2024.

sec.title: Interventions
sec.p: Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive tislelizumab, 200 mg, intravenously or placebo every 3 weeks, both with gemcitabine and cisplatin for 4 to 6 cycles. Participants in the placebo arm could cross over to tislelizumab monotherapy at disease progression.

sec.title: Main Outcomes and Measures
sec.p: The primary end point was progression-free survival (PFS) assessed by an independent review committee. The primary hypothesis (PFS superiority for tislelizumab vs placebo) was specified in the protocol prior to data collection. Secondary end points included overall survival (OS), PFS after next-line therapy, and safety.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of 263 included participants, 206 (78.3%) were male, and the median (range) age was 50 (23-74) years; the median (range) follow-up was 27.5 (0.1-53.0) months. A total of 131 were randomized to the tislelizumab group and 132 to the placebo group. Tislelizumab plus chemotherapy demonstrated improved PFS vs placebo plus chemotherapy (median PFS, 9.6 months [95% CI, 7.6-11.6] vs 7.4 months [95% CI, 5.6-7.6]; hazard ratio [HR], 0.53; 95% CI, 0.39-0.71). The median OS was 45.3 months (95% CI, 33.4 to not estimable) vs 31.8 months (95% CI, 25.0 to not estimable), respectively (HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.51-1.05). Rank-preserving structural failure time analysis (HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.27-1.19) and 2-stage crossover-adjusted analysis (HR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.40-0.97) showed greater OS benefit. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 133 of 133 participants (100%) in the tislelizumab arm and 129 of 130 participants (99.2%) in the placebo arm, with comparable grade 3 or higher adverse event rates. Immune-mediated adverse events were more frequent with tislelizumab (71 [53.4%] vs 49 [37.7%]) but mostly of grades 1 or 2. High B-cell gene expression was associated with greater OS benefit (HR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.23-0.74).

sec.title: Conclusions and Relevance
sec.p: In this secondary analysis of the RATIONALE-309 randomized clinical trial, after 3 years of follow-up, tislelizumab plus chemotherapy provided sustained PFS and meaningful OS improvement vs placebo plus chemotherapy in recurrent or metastatic NPC, with an acceptable safety profile. Greater benefit was observed in participants with activated immune signatures, especially high B-cell expression.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) affects 120 000 people annually, causing 73 000 deaths, predominantly in Asia.1 Recent advances in treatment—including the preliminary evidence of anti–programmed cell death 1 protein (PD-1) antibody treatment (tislelizumab, sintilimab) combined with induction chemotherapy, followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy and adjuvant anti–PD-1 antibody treatment2,3 or adjuvant anti–PD-1 antibody treatment (camrelizumab) after curative chemoradiation4— may provide improved outcomes for patients with locoregionally advanced NPC,5,6,7 with 5-year survival rates reaching 80%5 and 5-year local control rates of 74% to 90%.6 However, the prognosis for recurrent or metastatic NPC remains poor and thus represents a substantial unmet medical need.8 Immunotherapy, particularly anti–PD-1 antibodies combined with chemotherapy, has shown promising antitumor activity in treatment-naive recurrent or metastatic NPC.9,10,11 Phase 3 trials have demonstrated that this combination significantly prolongs progression-free survival (PFS) in the treatment-naive recurrent or metastatic NPC setting.12,13,14 Consequently, international guidelines now recommend this approach as the preferred first-line treatment for recurrent or metastatic NPC.15,16

The phase 3 RATIONALE-309 trial evaluated tislelizumab vs placebo, both combined with gemcitabine plus cisplatin, as a first-line treatment for recurrent or metastatic NPC. At the protocol-defined interim analysis (data cutoff, March 26, 2021; median study follow-up, 10.0 months), the RATIONALE-309 trial demonstrated a significant improvement in independent review committee–assessed PFS (primary end point) and a trend of overall survival (OS) benefit (secondary end point) in the tislelizumab vs placebo arm.14 First-line tislelizumab plus chemotherapy is now approved by the European Commission and the Chinese National Medical Products Administration for recurrent or metastatic NPC.17,18

To assess the long-term benefits of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy as a first-line treatment for recurrent or metastatic NPC, 3-year follow-up data from the RATIONALE-309 trial, including mature OS results were analyzed. An exploratory gene expression profiling (GEP) analysis of tumor microenvironments (TMEs) was also conducted to identify potential response biomarkers.

sec.title: Study Design and Participants
sec.p: The RATIONALE-309 study was a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 randomized clinical trial conducted at 42 sites across Asia. The study design has been described previously.14 Briefly, between April 18, 2019, and September 30, 2020, treatment-naive participants with histologically or cytologically confirmed recurrent or metastatic NPC were randomized (1:1) to receive tislelizumab, 200 mg, intravenously or placebo once every 3 weeks, plus chemotherapy (gemcitabine, 1 g/m2, intravenously on days 1 and 8 and cisplatin, 80 mg/m2, on day 1). Chemotherapy was administered once every 3 weeks for 4 to 6 cycles at the investigators’ discretion. Randomization, using interactive response technology, was stratified by sex and liver metastatic status. Treatment continued until disease progression (assessed by independent review committee per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors [RECIST] version 1.1), unacceptable toxic effects, or withdrawal. Participants in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm could continue tislelizumab monotherapy beyond investigator-assessed progression. Participants in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm could cross over to tislelizumab monotherapy after independent review committee–confirmed progression. Race was self-reported by participants at screening.

The trial conformed to the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use guidelines for Good Clinical Practice and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The RATIONALE-309 study protocol and amendments were approved by the institutional review board or independent ethics committee at each of the 42 participating sites; the trial protocol can be found in Supplement 1, and the statistical analysis plan can be found in Supplement 2. All participants provided written informed consent. This study followed the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) reporting guideline. Safety monitoring was performed by an independent data monitoring committee. Additional details regarding the study design are included in the eMethods in Supplement 3.

sec.title: End Points
sec.p: The primary end point was independent review committee–assessed PFS (defined as time from randomization to disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first per RECIST version 1.1) in the intent-to-treat analysis set. Secondary end points included OS (time from randomization to death from any cause), PFS after next-line therapy (time from randomization to second or subsequent disease progression after initiation of new anticancer therapy or death from any cause, whichever occurred first, assessed by investigator), and safety. Adverse events (AEs) were graded according to National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. Immune-mediated AEs were determined using a predefined programmatic algorithmic approach and were based on a list of preferred terms, without manual medical adjudication. Biomarker analysis was an exploratory end point.

sec.title: GEP
sec.p: GEP was performed using the EdgeSeq Precision Immuno-Oncology Panel (HTG Molecular Diagnostics; 1392 genes), sequenced on the NextSeq 500 System (Illumina), with log2-transformed counts analyzed for B-cell signatures via single-sample gene set enrichment analysis and clustered using ConsensusClusterPlus version 1.52.0 (Bioconductor), as described in a previous publication.14 For additional details, refer to the eMethods in Supplement 3.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Time-to-event end points were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, with the 95% CIs for median PFS, OS, and PFS after next-line therapy estimated by the Brookmeyer and Crowley method. Event-free rates were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method, with 95% CIs estimated using the Greenwood formula. The stratified Cox proportional hazards model (stratified by sex and liver metastatic status) was used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs. The rank-preserving structural failure time model (RPSFTM)19 and 2-stage method20 were used to assess the impact of in-study crossover of participants from the placebo-chemotherapy arm to tislelizumab monotherapy on postprogression OS. Additional details are included in the eMethods in Supplement 3. For the 2-stage method, 95% CIs were generated using bootstrapping to reflect uncertainty in both survival times and the adjustment process.21

The intent-to-treat analysis set included all randomized participants. Safety was assessed in all randomized participants who received any dose of the study drug, with analysis based on the treatment regimen received, using descriptive statistics. The exploratory biomarker analyses were performed in the biomarker-evaluable analysis set (all randomized participants with evaluable data for the respective biomarker, analyzed according to their randomized treatment). Biomarker analyses were based on the data cutoff dataset of December 8, 2023. Analyses were performed using SAS version 9.3 or higher (SAS Institute). Data were analyzed from December 2023 to January 2024.

sec.title: Patient Demographic and Baseline Characteristics
sec.p: Of 263 included participants, 57 (21.7%) were female, 206 (78.3%) were male, and the median (range) age was 50 (23-74) years. A total of 131 participants were randomized to tislelizumab plus chemotherapy and 132 were randomized to placebo plus chemotherapy. At 3-year follow-up (data cutoff, December 8, 2023), the median (range) study follow-up was 27.5 (0.1-53.0) months. All 263 participants were included in the intent-to-treat and safety analysis sets (Figure 1). Participant demographic and baseline characteristics were similar between arms and representative of the target population (Table 1). Most participants (248 [94.3%]) were from China. Primary metastatic disease was present in 86 participants (32.7%), while 165 (62.7%) had recurrence after prior treatment for local disease.

sec.title: Treatment Exposure
sec.p: A total of 133 participants received tislelizumab and 130 received placebo. The median (range) exposure was longer for tislelizumab than placebo (45.7 [1.1-230.7] weeks vs 33.9 [2.4-202.4] weeks); the median (range) number of cycles was also higher (14 [1-69] cycles vs 10 [1-58] cycles). The median (range) relative dose intensity (actual dose received compared with the planned dose) was 95.7% (45.9%-102.8%) for tislelizumab and 95.5% (67.5%-100.9%) for placebo.

In the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm, 78 of 131 participants (59.5%) received subsequent systemic anticancer therapies, predominantly chemotherapy. In the placebo plus chemotherapy arm, 69 of 132 participants (52.3%) crossed over to tislelizumab monotherapy after independent review committee–confirmed progression, 32 of 132 (24.2%) received subsequent systemic anticancer therapies, and 18 of 132 (13.6%) received subsequent immunotherapy (excluding tislelizumab crossover). Overall, 74 of 132 participants (56.1%) in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm received tislelizumab as subsequent therapy, including 69 who crossed over. Progressive disease was the main reason for discontinuing tislelizumab after crossover (50 of 69 [72.5%]) (eTable 1 in Supplement 3).

sec.title: PFS
sec.p: The 3-year follow-up efficacy analysis demonstrated sustained and clinically meaningful PFS improvement among participants who received tislelizumab plus chemotherapy vs placebo plus chemotherapy (stratified HR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.39-0.71). The median PFS was 9.6 months (95% CI, 7.6-11.6) for the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm vs 7.4 months (95% CI, 5.6-7.6) for the placebo plus chemotherapy arm (Figure 2). Consistent PFS benefit was observed in almost all participant subgroups, regardless of liver metastatic status, baseline Epstein-Barr virus DNA level, and tumor cell (TC) programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression level (eFigure 1 in Supplement 3).

caption.p: The data cutoff was December 8, 2023. In the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm, there were 95 PFS events (72.5%) over a median of 9.6 months (95% CI, 7.6-11.6); in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm, there were 106 PFS events (80.3%) over a median of 7.4 months (95% CI, 5.6-7.6) (hazard ratio, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.39-0.71). The hazard ratio was estimated from a stratified Cox model with the placebo plus chemotherapy arm as a reference group. In the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm, the 12-month and 24-month PFS rate was 35.1% (95% CI, 26.6-43.8) and 23.5% (95% CI, 16.1-31.7), respectively; in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm, the 12-month and 24-month PFS rate was 10.2% (95% CI, 5.4-16.8) and 7.3% (95% CI, 3.4-13.3), respectively. Circles represent censored participants.

sec.p: An exploratory analysis of interim and 3-year follow-up data showed a clinically meaningful improvement in PFS regardless of TC PD-L1 expression levels. HRs ranged from 0.38 (95% CI, 0.20-0.72) to 0.55 (95% CI, 0.33-0.93) across low and high TC PD-L1 expression groups, suggesting clinical benefit independent of TC PD-L1 expression (eTable 2 and eFigure 2 in Supplement 3).

sec.title: OS
sec.p: As of the study end date (December 8, 2023), with a median survival follow-up of 41.4 months (95% CI, 40.1-42.2) in the tislelizumab arm and 40.8 months (95% CI, 39.8-41.7) in the placebo arm, participants treated with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy experienced clinically meaningful improvement in OS vs those treated with placebo plus chemotherapy (stratified HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.51-1.05), despite high crossover in the placebo arm (69 of 132 [52.3%]) (Figure 3). The median OS was 45.3 months (95% CI, 33.4 to not estimable [NE]) for tislelizumab plus chemotherapy vs 31.8 months (95% CI, 25.0-NE) for placebo plus chemotherapy. Exploratory analysis at 3-year follow-up showed improved OS with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy across PD-L1 TC expression cutoffs (TCs ≥10%: HR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.41-1.05; TCs <10%: HR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.36-1.27) (eFigure 3 in Supplement 3).

caption.title: Overall Survival (OS) in the Intent-to-Treat Analysis Set
caption.p: The data cutoff was December 8, 2023. In the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm, there were 55 OS events (42.0%) over a median of 45.3 months (95% CI, 33.4 to not estimable); in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm, there were 64 OS events (48.5%) over a median of 31.8 months (95% CI, 25.0 to not estimable) (hazard ratio, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.51-1.05). The hazard ratio was estimated from a stratified Cox model with the placebo plus chemotherapy arm as a reference group. In the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm, the 12-month, 24-month, and 36-month OS rate was 89.6% (95% CI, 82.8-93.8), 69.4% (95% CI, 60.4-76.8), and 55.6% (95% CI, 46.0-64.1), respectively; in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm, the 12-month, 24-month, and 36-month OS rate was 84.9% (95% CI, 77.1-90.2), 59.6% (95% CI, 50.1-67.9), and 46.4% (95% CI, 36.9-55.3), respectively. Circles represent censored participants.

sec.p: Two supportive OS analyses adjusted for the crossover effect. The RPSFTM approach yielded a stratified HR of 0.56 (95% CI, 0.27-1.19) favoring tislelizumab plus chemotherapy vs placebo plus chemotherapy, with an adjusted median OS for the placebo plus chemotherapy arm of 23.0 months (95% CI, 19.1-31.6) (eFigure 4A in Supplement 3). The 2-stage approach resulted in a stratified HR of 0.62 (95% CI, 0.40-0.97), with an adjusted median OS for placebo plus chemotherapy of 27.0 months (95% CI, 20.0-36.8) (eFigure 4B in Supplement 3).

sec.title: PFS After Next-Line Therapy
sec.p: Per investigator assessment, the median PFS after next-line therapy was 45.3 months (95% CI, 31.5-NE) in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm vs 20.5 months (95% CI, 13.9-27.2) in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm (unstratified HR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.34-0.75) (eFigure 5 in Supplement 3).

sec.title: Safety and Tolerability
sec.p: The safety analysis included 133 participants in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm and 130 in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm. Treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs) occurred in 133 of 133 participants (100%) in the tislelizumab arm and 129 of 130 participants (99.2%) in the placebo arm. Rates of grade 3 or higher TEAEs and serious TEAEs were comparable between arms (Table 2). The most frequent TEAEs were anemia, decreased neutrophil count, and decreased white blood cell count (eTable 3 in Supplement 3). Serious TEAEs occurring in 2% or more of participants are listed in eTable 4 in Supplement 3. Permanent discontinuation of any study treatment component due to TEAEs occurred in 22 participants (16.5%) in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm and in 14 (10.8%) in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm (Table 2; eTable 5 in Supplement 3). TEAEs leading to death were reported in 6 participants (4.5%) in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm (2 treatment-related) and 2 (1.5%) in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm (both treatment-related) (Table 2; eTable 6 in Supplement 3). In the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm, treatment-related deaths were due to myelodysplastic syndrome (related to chemotherapy and tislelizumab) and death with unknown cause (related to chemotherapy only). In the placebo plus chemotherapy arm, deaths were due to arrhythmia and hypernatremia (chemotherapy-related) and death with unknown cause (related to placebo and chemotherapy). Immune-mediated AEs were more frequent for tislelizumab plus chemotherapy (any grade, 71 [53.4%]; grade 3 or higher, 6 [4.5%]) than for placebo plus chemotherapy (any grade, 49 [37.7%]; grade 3 or higher, 1 [0.8%]). The most common immune-mediated AEs were skin adverse reactions and hypothyroidism. No grade 4 or 5 immune-mediated AEs were reported (eTable 7 in Supplement 3). Serious immune-mediated AEs occurred in 5 participants (3.8%) in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm and 1 (0.8%) in the placebo-chemotherapy arm. Immune-mediated AEs led to tislelizumab discontinuation in 4 participants (3.0%) and to treatment modifications in 7 participants (5.3%). Systemic corticosteroids were used for immune-mediated AE management in 8 participants (6.0%) treated with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy and 7 (5.4%) treated with placebo plus chemotherapy. No participants received immunosuppressants.

sec.title: Exploratory Biomarker Analysis
sec.p: In the hot TME subgroup, the median OS was not reached (95% CI, 34.9-NE) in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm vs 36.8 months (95% CI, 23.0-NE) in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm (HR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.40-1.08) (eFigure 6A in Supplement 3). In the cold TME subgroup, the median OS was 35.1 months (95% CI, 19.7-NE) vs 26.7 months (95% CI, 19.8-NE), respectively (HR, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.51-1.60) (eFigure 6B in Supplement 3). This suggests potential benefit in both hot and cold TME tumors, with potentially greater benefit in hot TME tumors. Consistent with the OS findings, PFS analysis also demonstrated benefit with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy in both hot TME (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.31-0.67) and cold TME (HR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.49-1.24) subgroups, with a more pronounced effect in the hot TME subgroup (eFigure 8 in Supplement 3).

GEP signature analyses (representing both immune cell and TC characteristics) revealed associations between OS benefit and activated immune signatures (including B-cell, T-cell, and activated dendritic cells) favoring tislelizumab plus chemotherapy, while these same signatures were weakly or reversely correlated in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm (eFigure 11A in Supplement 3). These results are consistent with the observed correlations between GEP signatures and PFS data (eFigure 11B in Supplement 3). Clinically meaningful OS benefit observed in participants treated with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy was enriched in the high B-cell signature subgroup (HR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.23-0.74), while the low B-cell signature subgroup showed an OS HR of 1.14 (95% CI, 0.69-1.90) (eFigures 7 and 10A in Supplement 3). In the high B-cell signature subgroup, the median OS was not reached (95% CI, 43.0-NE) in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm and 31.6 months (95% CI, 20.1-40.6) in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm (eFigure 7A in Supplement 3). In the low B-cell signature subgroup, the median OS was 33.4 months (95% CI, 23.7-NE) in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm and not reached (95% CI, 19.8-NE) in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm (eFigure 7B in Supplement 3). Clinically meaningful PFS benefits were observed in both the high B-cell signature subgroup (HR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.31-0.72) and low B-cell signature subgroup (HR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.41-0.93) (eFigures 9 and 10B in Supplement 3). High expressors of representative B-cell marker genes (ie, CD19, MS4A1, CD79B, and CXCR5) showed clinically meaningful OS improvement with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy (eFigure 10A in Supplement 3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: After 3 years of follow-up (ie, with an additional 17 months of follow-up from the interim analysis), the phase 3 RATIONALE-309 trial demonstrated sustained efficacy benefits of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy vs placebo plus chemotherapy in participants with recurrent or metastatic NPC. The PFS benefit persisted (HR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.39-0.71) and was consistent with the interim analysis findings (HR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.38-0.73; data cutoff, March 26, 2021).14 With extended follow-up, participants receiving tislelizumab plus chemotherapy showed a clinically meaningful improvement in OS (HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.51-1.05) despite a high crossover rate (69 of 132 [52.3%]) in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm. Two supportive OS analyses, adjusting for crossover, demonstrated similar HR estimates (RPSFTM: HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.27-1.19; 2-stage method: HR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.40-0.97), suggesting that crossover may have affected the measured treatment effect. PFS after next-line therapy analysis confirmed maintained benefit for participants who received tislelizumab-chemotherapy and subsequent anticancer treatment (HR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.34-0.75), underscoring its durable therapeutic effect in first-line treatment.

Despite the unique design of the RATIONALE-309 trial, including crossover and PFS after next-line therapy data collection, the long-term efficacy of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy aligns with that seen in other phase 3 trials of PD-1 inhibitors plus chemotherapy for first-line recurrent or metastatic NPC and builds on recent advances in the adjuvant setting.5,6,7 The final analysis of the JUPITER-02 trial found significantly improved PFS (HR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.37-0.73) and OS (HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.45-0.89) with toripalimab plus chemotherapy vs placebo plus chemotherapy for patients with recurrent or metastatic NPC.12 The interim analysis of the CAPTAIN-1st trial demonstrated favorable outcomes for camrelizumab plus chemotherapy (PFS: HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.39-0.76; OS: HR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.41-1.11) vs placebo plus chemotherapy, although the final analyses with mature OS data have yet to be reported. These trials support integrating PD-1 inhibitors with chemotherapy for first-line recurrent or metastatic NPC. While OS benefits in these trials appeared numerically better than in the RATIONALE-309 trial, they lacked crossover designs. Considering the supportive analysis of the RATIONALE-309 trial, all 3 studies showed similar outcomes. The median OS observed in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm of RATIONALE-309 (31.8 months; 95% CI, 25.0-NE) aligns with previously reported outcomes for chemotherapy alone in phase 3 trials, which ranged from 18.6 to 29.1 months.22,23 Participants treated with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy achieved a higher median OS of 45.3 months (95% CI, 33.4-NE), underscoring its improved efficacy.

While the PFS improvement with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy vs placebo plus chemotherapy in this study appears relatively modest (9.6 months [95% CI, 7.6-11.6] vs 7.4 months [95% CI, 5.6-7.6]), the OS benefit was more pronounced (45.3 months [95% CI, 33.4-NE] vs 31.8 months [95% CI, 25.0-NE]). This discordance highlights that while the immunotherapy-chemotherapy combination provides superior initial disease control (reflected by PFS), its primary value lies in conferring a sustained survival advantage (reflected by OS). This can be attributed to the unique mechanism of action of immunotherapy, which induces durable antitumor immune responses and establishes immunologic memory, allowing a subset of patients to experience long-term disease control even after the initial period measured by PFS. This phenomenon of a delayed separation of the OS curves24 is consistent with observations from the JUPITER-02 trial and suggests a common benefit pattern with immune therapy in recurrent or metastatic NPC. This sustained benefit is driven by the enduring effects of immune activation,25 which can lead to long-term remission even after initial progression and is influenced by confounding factors, such as crossover therapy in the control arm, which can attenuate the measured OS difference.24 The significant PFS after next-line therapy improvement (45.3 months [95% CI, 31.5-NE] vs 20.5 months [95% CI, 13.9-27.2]) further reinforces the durability of first-line benefit while accounting for subsequent treatment efficacy.

The long-term safety profile of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy was consistent with known risks, with no new safety signals identified. TEAEs leading to permanent discontinuation were slightly more frequent in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm (22 [16.5%]) than in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm (14 [10.8%]), likely due to longer treatment exposure. As expected, given the immune mechanism of tislelizumab, immune-mediated AEs of any grade were more common in the tislelizumab plus chemotherapy arm (71 [53.4%] vs 49 [37.7%]), but most were grade 1 or 2 in severity, and no immune-mediated AE-related deaths occurred. The immune-mediated AE profile observed was similar to the common immune-mediated AEs known to occur with immune checkpoint inhibitors.26

Our analysis showed clinically meaningful efficacy benefits of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy across PD-L1 TC expression subgroups, supporting previous findings that PD-L1 TC expression may not definitively predict response to first-line anti–PD-1 chemotherapy in recurrent or metastatic NPCs.27 In the interim RATIONALE-309 analysis reported by Yang et al,14 a GEP analysis (using gene signatures representing different TMEs) was performed to identify biomarkers for immunochemotherapy response in recurrent or metastatic NPC. This 3-year follow-up analysis leveraged the same gene signatures to correlate TME categories with OS. Novel biomarker analyses showed associations between OS benefit and both the hot TME subgroup and activated immune signatures (B-cell, T-cell, and dendritic cell), favoring tislelizumab plus chemotherapy. These align with previous PFS benefit biomarker findings for tislelizumab plus chemotherapy.14 Among various cancer types, NPC exhibits the highest levels of tumor-infiltrating B cells,28 with B-cell signatures and subpopulations correlating significantly with disease outcomes.29 Key B-cell–related genes (eg, CD19, MS4A1 [CD20], CD79A, CD79B, IGHD, and FCRL4) were identified as part of a prognostic signature in NPC, suggesting an important role for functional B cells in antitumor immunity.29,30 Aggregated B cells within tumors usually indicate diverse immune cell types and tertiary lymphoid structures, enhancing antitumor immune responses.31,32 In the current study, tislelizumab plus chemotherapy demonstrated PFS benefits in both high (HR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.31-0.72) and low (HR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.41-0.93) B-cell signature expression subgroups, with OS benefit observed only in the high B-cell signature subgroup (HR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.23-0.74). These findings align with previous studies linking B-cell signature genes to better NPC survival.29,33 For instance, Lv et al demonstrated that higher expression of B-cell–related genes was positively associated with survival in participants with NPC who were treated with chemotherapy.33 Our results extend these observations to immunotherapy, suggesting that B-cell signatures may serve as predictive biomarkers for anti–PD-1 treatment in NPC, addressing limitations of traditional PD-L1 TC expression as a predictive marker. This large-scale randomized clinical trial provides evidence supporting the prospective validation of high B-cell signatures as predictive biomarkers for antitumor immunotherapies in recurrent or metastatic NPC. These findings indicate the potential for biomarker-informed strategies to optimize patient selection for anti−PD-L1 therapies in recurrent or metastatic NPC. Such strategies could improve treatment outcomes for patients likely to benefit from anti–PD-1 therapy.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This study has limitations. It was conducted exclusively in Asian regions, potentially limiting generalizability to areas where keratinizing carcinoma is more common.34 Results from certain subgroups (eg, participants 65 years and older, participants with PD-L1 status not evaluable) should be interpreted with caution because they were exploratory with limited sample sizes, leading to variable HR estimates. The crossover design limits precise between-arm comparison of OS, although the median OS in the treatment arm was unaffected. Two supportive OS analyses addressed this limitation but have inherent constraints. The 2-stage model included only 37 participants from the control arm who progressed per independent review committee but did not cross over to receive tislelizumab and assumed no unmeasured confounders. The RPSFTM faced challenges due to differences in treatment initiation between arms. Despite those limitations, both approaches yielded comparable HR estimates, supporting the robustness of the OS results.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: At the 3-year follow-up of the RATIONALE-309 trial, participants with recurrent or metastatic NPC who received tislelizumab plus chemotherapy experienced sustained PFS benefits and clinically meaningful OS improvements as well as longer PFS after next-line therapy vs placebo plus chemotherapy, despite high crossover rates. The PFS improvement observed in the interim analysis has translated into a durable OS benefit. Safety remained acceptable, with manageable toxic effects. Exploratory GEP analysis identified potential response biomarkers, with participants exhibiting high B-cell signature expression showing clinically meaningful improvements in OS. These long-term efficacy and safety findings further support tislelizumab plus chemotherapy as an effective first-line recurrent or metastatic NPC treatment.
